questions.question: A music festival's network technician is documenting traffic that flows between internal segments, such as gate scanners reaching the ticketing servers. What is this traffic MOST accurately called?

options.A: East-west traffic
options.B: North-south traffic
options.C: Out-of-band traffic
options.D: Broadcast traffic

questions.key_concept: East-west traffic moves between systems inside the network; north-south traffic crosses the network's edge to or from outside.
questions.pre_read: Picture which traffic ever passes the festival's internet edge.
questions.correct_explanation: Traffic moving between systems inside the network, from segment to segment or server to server, is called east-west traffic, and internal segmentation rules exist mainly to control it. North-south is the runner-up because it is the paired term, but it means traffic entering or leaving the network through its edge, which perimeter firewalls watch.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it is the paired term. But north-south traffic crosses the network edge, in from or out to the internet, not between internal segments.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds like traffic outside the main path. But out-of-band means a separate channel, such as a dedicated management link.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because traffic can reach many devices. But a broadcast is one frame sent to every device on a local segment, not traffic between segments.

tips: Eliminate: C names a separate management channel, and D names one frame sent to every device on a segment.
Final two: A beats B because east-west traffic stays inside the network; north-south traffic crosses its edge.
Exam cue: east-west stays inside and is controlled by segmentation; north-south crosses the edge and meets the perimeter firewall.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-215 Section 2.1 (Limitations of Network Perimeter-based Protections: east-west traffic stays within the local network)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Traffic between internal segments is east-west; traffic into and out of the network is north-south' (notes 4.2.1 Network Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A candle maker's IT manager says the screened subnet holding its online shop needs no firewall rules on the internet side, since the shop is public. Which reply from the network technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: The inner firewall alone protects the screened subnet
options.B: Public servers are safer on the internal network instead
options.C: The outer firewall should expose only the shop's web ports
options.D: The outer firewall should allow everything but log each visit

questions.key_concept: A screened subnet is filtered on both sides: the internet reaches only named public services, and inside only through narrow paths.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else on the shop server an internet stranger could reach without outer rules.
questions.correct_explanation: A screened subnet is less trusted than the internal network, not unprotected. The outer firewall still lets the internet reach only the shop's named services, such as its web ports, and blocks everything else, so attackers cannot probe the server's other services. Allowing everything but logging it is the runner-up because logs help investigations, but logging records attacks without stopping any.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the inner firewall guards the internal network. But it does nothing for the shop server itself, which would face every probe from the internet.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the internal network is more trusted. But a public server there means one breach puts attackers inside, beside staff systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: logging every visit does help investigations. But it only records attacks; the server's other services stay open to the whole internet.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the shop server facing the whole internet, and B moves a public server inside, where one breach reaches staff systems.
Final two: C beats D because the outer firewall must allow only the shop's services; logging everything records attacks without stopping them.
Exam cue: the screened subnet sits between two sets of rules; the internet side still allows only the named public services.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 3.1 (Network Layouts with Firewalls: public-facing servers on the DMZ); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(5) (Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Firewall rules protect its internet side too. It is less trusted than the internal network, not unprotected' (notes 4.2.2 Firewall Zones and the Screened Subnet (DMZ)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A visitor's laptop in a spare lobby jack reached a trampoline park's staff VLAN; the system owner approves VLAN design, and procedure has the network technician shut unused ports. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Disable the lobby port, and record the change
options.B: Record it, and ask the system owner to redesign the VLAN
options.C: Move the staff VLAN onto a different IP address range
options.D: Have reception watch visitors near the lobby wall jacks

questions.key_concept: Unused switch ports should be disabled or put in an empty VLAN; when the procedure assigns this, the technician does it and records it.
questions.pre_read: Picture what any device plugged into a live spare port can reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Shutting unused ports is the technician's assigned task, so they disable the lobby port, record the change and apply the same check to other spare ports. A live but unused port is an open door to whatever VLAN it belongs to. Asking the system owner is the runner-up because the owner approves VLAN design, but this fix needs no redesign; the procedure already gives it to the technician.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the system owner does approve VLAN design. But closing an unused port is not a design change, and the procedure assigns it to the technician.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because separate address ranges look like separation. But the lobby port would still sit on the staff VLAN, whatever range it uses.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff can spot misuse. But watching people leaves the port live, and one unnoticed plug-in still reaches staff systems.

tips: Eliminate: C changes addresses while the lobby port stays on the staff VLAN, and D relies on people watching while the port stays live.
Final two: A beats B because the procedure gives this fix to the technician; the owner's design approval does not cover closing a spare port.
Exam cue: an owner in the stem is not an automatic escalation; if the procedure assigns you the task, do it and record it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Unused ports are disabled or put in an empty VLAN' (notes 4.2.3 Virtual LANs (VLANs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A cider maker's IT manager proposes retiring the internet edge firewall now that every server has micro-segmentation rules. Which reply from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agreed, since workload rules already block outside attackers
options.B: Keep both, since each one filters different traffic
options.C: Agreed, if the workload rules are reviewed every month
options.D: Swap the workload rules for VLANs and keep the edge firewall

questions.key_concept: Micro-segmentation adds to perimeter controls instead of replacing them; workload rules and the edge firewall protect different traffic.
questions.pre_read: List what the edge firewall stops that a server's own rules never see.
questions.correct_explanation: Micro-segmentation controls east-west traffic between workloads; the edge firewall filters what enters from the internet before it reaches anything, including laptops and printers that have no workload rules. They do different jobs, so defense in depth keeps both. Agreeing with monthly reviews is the runner-up because reviews keep workload rules accurate, but reviewed rules still cover only the servers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because workload rules do block unwanted connections. But they cover only the servers they sit on, and give up the edge's filtering of internet traffic.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: regular reviews keep workload rules accurate. But reviewed rules still cover only servers, and the edge layer they would replace does a different job.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because VLANs also separate systems. But VLANs group switch ports; they cannot separate two servers on the same VLAN, which workload rules can.

tips: Eliminate: A treats workload rules as a full perimeter, and D swaps them for VLANs, which cannot separate servers on the same VLAN.
Final two: B beats C because no review makes workload rules do the edge firewall's job; the two layers cover different traffic.
Exam cue: micro-segmentation adds to the perimeter; when one control is proposed to replace another, check whether they cover the same traffic.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 3.1.2 (ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'It adds to perimeter controls. Defense in depth keeps both the edge and the workload rules' (notes 4.2.4 Micro-Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Defense in depth
questions.question: A vintage clothing reseller's defenses are an edge firewall, an email filter and USB ports locked on its checkout computers. Which addition should the security team propose to BEST strengthen its defense in depth?

options.A: A second email filter from another vendor, run in series
options.B: A next-generation firewall to replace the current firewall
options.C: Monitoring to spot attacks, and backups to restore its data
options.D: Stricter edge firewall rules, with the vendor monitoring them

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth pairs prevention with detection and recovery, so an attack that gets past blocking controls is still found and undone.
questions.pre_read: Imagine one attack gets past all three controls. What happens next?
questions.correct_explanation: All three layers are preventive, so when an attack gets past them, nothing would notice it or recover from it. Defense in depth pairs prevention with detection and recovery: alert monitoring spots what slips through, and tested backups restore what is damaged. A second email filter is the runner-up because it is a genuinely separate layer, but it is one more preventive control of the same kind.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a second vendor's filter is an independent layer. But it is still prevention; when an attack gets through, nothing yet detects it or recovers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a newer firewall blocks more. But it replaces a layer instead of adding one, and the defenses remain prevention only.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tighter rules block more. But vendor monitoring of edge rules is still about the edge; nothing would detect or recover from an attack already inside.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps one firewall for another instead of adding a layer, and D only tightens and watches the same edge layer; neither detects an attack already inside or restores data.
Final two: C beats A because every current layer prevents; adding detection and recovery covers the day prevention fails, which a second filter does not.
Exam cue: depth means different kinds of control: prevent, detect and recover. If every layer only blocks, add one that notices or restores.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Prevention is paired with detection and recovery, such as monitoring and tested backups, for the day prevention fails' (notes 4.2.5 Defense in Depth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust components
questions.question: At a beekeeping cooperative adopting Zero Trust, an AI scheduling agent reads the member database over an old direct connection that no enforcement point covers. Which statement should the network technician report as MOST accurate?

options.A: The policy engine still judges each request the agent sends that way
options.B: The agent needs no checks, since it runs on the internal network
options.C: The path is safe enough if the agent's account has least privilege
options.D: Nothing along that path applies the policy to the agent's requests

questions.key_concept: A Zero Trust policy protects only resources behind an enforcement point; any path around it, used by people or AI agents, escapes the policy.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the agent's request would have to pass for a decision to be made.
questions.correct_explanation: In Zero Trust, the policy engine decides and an enforcement point in front of the resource carries out the decision. A path with no enforcement point never asks for a decision, so the agent's requests skip the policy entirely. Least privilege is the runner-up because it limits what the agent can do, but its requests are still never checked against identity, context or logging rules.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the policy engine makes every decision. But it only hears of requests that an enforcement point passes to it, and this path has none.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the agent is the cooperative's own software on its own network. But Zero Trust grants nothing for network location, to people or to AI agents.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: least privilege does limit the damage. But the requests still bypass the policy, so nothing checks context or enforces the rules on that path.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes the policy engine sees requests no enforcement point sends it, and B trusts the agent for being on the internal network.
Final two: D beats C because limited rights do not bring the path under the policy; every protected resource needs an enforcement point.
Exam cue: in Zero Trust, a resource reachable without passing an enforcement point is outside the policy, whoever or whatever connects.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 3 (Logical Components of Zero Trust Architecture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A resource with no enforcement point in front of it sits outside the policy's protection' (notes 4.2.7 Zero Trust Architecture Components). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Network access control
questions.question: A lumber yard is adding network access control (NAC), and the network technician must explain what its posture check examines. Which description is MOST accurate?

options.A: The device's MAC address, checked against a known-device list
options.B: The device's health, such as its patch level and antivirus
options.C: The user's password strength and when it was last changed
options.D: The device's certificate, proving it belongs to the company

questions.key_concept: NAC posture checks examine device health, such as patches, antivirus and encryption; identity is checked separately, often by certificate.
questions.pre_read: Separate proving what a device is from checking what condition it is in.
questions.correct_explanation: A posture check looks at device health, such as patch level, antivirus status and disk encryption, before NAC grants access, and a device that fails goes to remediation. The certificate check is the runner-up because many NAC setups use one too, but that step authenticates the device, proving what it is; posture asks whether it is healthy enough to admit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because NAC does identify devices. But MAC addresses are easy to copy, and a known address says nothing about the device's health.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because passwords matter at sign-in. But posture is about the device's condition, not the user's password history.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: many NAC setups check a certificate as well. But that proves which device it is; posture checks whether it is patched and protected.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a copyable address, and C describes a password rule, not the device's condition.
Final two: B beats D because a certificate proves identity, while posture checks health: patches, antivirus and encryption.
Exam cue: NAC asks three things: who are you, what are you, and are you healthy? Posture is the health question.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: An airport shuttle service's AI experiment servers share a segment with its live demand model and can overwrite the model directly. Which change should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Move the experiments to a segment filtered from production
options.B: Keep one segment, since every server there is internal
options.C: Back up the live model nightly so it can be restored
options.D: Put a stricter edge firewall in front of the live model

questions.key_concept: AI development and production run on separate segments with filtered links, so experiments cannot reach or change live models.
questions.pre_read: Picture one experiment server being compromised and what it could reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Experiment servers are less locked down than production, so a careless test or a compromised experiment server can change the live model directly. Putting experiments on their own segment, with rules that allow only an approved release path into production, removes that reach. Nightly backups are the runner-up because they help recovery, but a poisoned or overwritten model could run for hours before anyone restores it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because all the servers are the service's own. But internal does not mean trusted; weaker experiment servers become an easy path to the live model.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: backups help recovery after damage. But they leave the experiments able to change the live model, which could run wrong for hours first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firewalls protect systems. But the edge firewall sees internet traffic, not experiment servers on the same internal segment.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts servers because they are internal, and D adds an edge control that never sees traffic inside the segment.
Final two: A beats C because separating the segments stops the change happening; a backup only helps after the live model is already wrong.
Exam cue: keep AI experiments on their own segment, away from production models and data; internal is not the same as trusted.
