questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust principles
questions.question: A moving company's IT manager says that once it adopts Zero Trust, the internal firewall zones and network segments can be removed. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Segments can go, since every request will be verified anyway
options.B: Segments can go once Zero Trust adds multifactor sign-in for staff
options.C: Zero Trust keeps segments, drawing boundaries closer to resources
options.D: Segments stay, but only to keep outside attackers off the network

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust relies on fine-grained segmentation, moving boundaries closer to each resource rather than removing them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what limits a verified account's reach once it is inside.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero Trust does not remove boundaries; it moves them closer to each resource, relying on fine-grained segmentation so that a verified user still reaches only what they need. Keeping segments only against outsiders is the runner-up: it keeps them, but for the wrong reason, since segmentation's main job under Zero Trust is limiting an intruder already inside.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because Zero Trust does verify every request. But verification works alongside fine-grained segments; it does not replace them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because multifactor sign-in is central to Zero Trust. But it proves who is asking, while segments limit what a verified or stolen account can reach.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it rightly keeps the segments. But their main value is internal, limiting how far an intruder already inside can move, which Zero Trust depends on.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both remove segments, though Zero Trust relies on fine-grained segmentation alongside verification and multifactor sign-in.
Final two: C beats D because Zero Trust uses segments mainly against movement inside, by drawing boundaries around each resource.
Exam cue: Zero Trust moves boundaries closer to resources; it does not remove them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 3.1.2 (ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation); NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Zero Trust removes the need for network segmentation' (exam trap, notes 4.2.6 Zero Trust Principles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust components
questions.question: At a telecom company adopting Zero Trust, the policy engine revokes an AI support agent's access mid-session after flagging risky behavior. What should the policy enforcement point MOST accurately do?

options.A: Let the open session finish, then block the agent's next request
options.B: Weigh the agent's behavior itself, and decide whether to agree
options.C: End the agent's open session to the resource it was using
options.D: Log the revocation, and keep the session open for review

questions.key_concept: A Zero Trust enforcement point carries out the decision point's rulings, including ending an open session when access is revoked.
questions.pre_read: Separate which component decides from which one acts on the decision.
questions.correct_explanation: In a Zero Trust architecture, the policy engine decides and the policy administrator passes the result on; the enforcement point carries it out, enabling, monitoring and, when a decision changes, terminating the connection. Letting the session finish is the runner-up: it blocks future requests, but trust is judged continuously, so a revoked agent keeps no access it already has.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: blocking the next request does stop future access. But Zero Trust checks continuously, and the revocation applies now, so the open session must end too.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the enforcement point sees the traffic. But it carries out decisions; judging the request is the policy engine's job.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records matter. But logging while the session stays open leaves the agent with access the policy has already withdrawn.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the decision to the enforcement point, which only carries decisions out, and D leaves revoked access running.
Final two: C beats A because a changed decision ends the session now; Zero Trust does not wait for the next request.
Exam cue: the decision point decides and the enforcement point enforces, including ending sessions when the decision changes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 3 (Logical Components of Zero Trust Architecture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The enforcement point allows or blocks the session, and ends it if a later decision changes' (notes 4.2.7 Zero Trust Architecture Components). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Network access control
questions.question: A post office's network access control (NAC) blocks any laptop that fails its posture check, so staff with missed updates cannot even download the fixes. Which change should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Move failing laptops to a quarantine network for updates
options.B: Let failing laptops join the network, and alert the help desk
options.C: Check posture once a month instead of at each connection
options.D: Turn off posture checks for laptops with missed updates

questions.key_concept: A failed posture check should limit a device to what it needs to get healthy; blocking it outright strands it without its fixes.
questions.pre_read: Ask how a failing laptop could ever get the fix it needs.
questions.correct_explanation: The usual design does not simply block a device that fails its health check: it quarantines it on a remediation network that reaches only the fixes, so the laptop can be updated and admitted again. Letting laptops on and alerting the help desk is the runner-up: it keeps staff working, but unhealthy laptops would reach the full network until someone acts.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it does keep staff working and gets the laptops fixed. But until someone acts, unhealthy laptops reach the whole network, which posture checks exist to prevent.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fewer checks mean fewer lockouts. But a laptop that loses its updates or antivirus between checks would roam the full network for weeks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it ends the lockouts. But it removes the health check, so laptops with missing updates join the network unchecked.

tips: Eliminate: C checks device health too rarely to keep unhealthy laptops off, and D drops the posture check itself.
Final two: A beats B because quarantine lets laptops get their fixes without reaching the full network while unhealthy.
Exam cue: in NAC, failing devices are remediated, not just blocked or waved through.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.7 (Network Access Control: health checks and limited access for remediation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Devices that fail a posture check should simply be blocked' (exam trap, notes 4.2.8 Network Access Control (NAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: A coin dealer's security manager owns exceptions to the outbound block on its AI training segment, and a data scientist wants uploads allowed to an unapproved AI service. What should the network technician do FIRST?

options.A: Allow that one service for the job, then tell the security manager
options.B: Ask the security manager to decide on the outbound request
options.C: Open outbound internet for the segment until the job is done
options.D: Copy the data to a laptop and upload it from the office

questions.key_concept: AI training segments restrict outbound traffic so data cannot reach unapproved services; exceptions go to whoever owns that rule.
questions.pre_read: Ask who may grant exceptions to the outbound block.
questions.correct_explanation: The outbound block keeps training data from reaching unapproved outside services, and exceptions to it belong to the security manager, so the technician asks the manager to decide rather than granting it themselves. Allowing just that one service and reporting afterwards is the runner-up: it is narrow and honest, but it still grants an exception the technician has no authority to make, and the data has already left.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: one narrow, reported exception sounds careful. But exceptions are the security manager's to grant, and once the upload runs, the training data has already left.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it unblocks the job fast. But open outbound traffic from an AI segment is exactly how training data leaks to unapproved services.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids changing the firewall. But it moves the training data off the controlled segment and goes around the block entirely.

tips: Eliminate: C opens all outbound traffic from the AI segment, and D carries the training data around the block on a laptop.
Final two: B beats A because only the security manager can grant exceptions, and a narrow upload still sends the data out first.
Exam cue: when a request needs an exception the rule's owner controls, ask the owner before acting, however narrow the change.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(5) (Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Outbound traffic is restricted, so data cannot reach unapproved outside AI services or storage' (notes 4.2.9 Segmenting AI Development Environments). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Length evened out (4 Nov 2026, blind re-test): the key is no longer the lone longest or shortest option by a wide margin.

questions.question: A fencing academy's coaches reach the same cloud booking service from laptops, tablets and phones over the internet, wherever they are. Which essential cloud characteristic does the IT coordinator see MOST directly here?

options.A: Broad network access
options.B: Resource pooling
options.C: Server virtualization
options.D: On-demand self-service

questions.key_concept: Broad network access means a cloud service is reachable over the network, through standard means, from many kinds of devices.
questions.pre_read: Match the clue in the scenario to one of the five characteristics.
questions.correct_explanation: Broad network access means the service is available over the network through standard mechanisms, from many kinds of devices such as laptops, tablets and phones. Resource pooling is the runner-up: NIST does describe a sense of location independence there, but that is about the customer not knowing where the provider's resources sit, not about reaching the service from anywhere.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: pooling does carry a sense of location independence. But that describes not knowing where the provider's resources sit, not reaching the service from many devices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because virtualization powers most clouds. But it is a technology that makes pooling possible, not one of the five essential characteristics.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because coaches use the service without calling anyone. But self-service is about setting up resources without provider help, not reaching the service from many devices.

tips: Eliminate: C is a technology behind clouds, not one of the five characteristics, and D is about setting up resources without provider help.
Final two: A beats B because the clue is many devices reaching the service over the network; pooling's location independence is about where resources sit.
Exam cue: 'any device, over the network' is broad network access; 'shared hardware' is resource pooling.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: essential characteristics)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Match the clue to the characteristic' (notes 4.3.1 The Five Essential Characteristics of Cloud Computing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A glassblowing studio's IT technician runs a test virtual machine inside an application on their laptop's ordinary operating system. Which kind of virtualization is this MOST accurately?

options.A: Bare metal (Type 1) virtualization
options.B: Container-based virtualization
options.C: Serverless computing
options.D: Hosted (Type 2) virtualization

questions.key_concept: A hosted (Type 2) hypervisor runs on an ordinary operating system; a bare metal (Type 1) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware.
questions.pre_read: Ask what sits directly under the hypervisor on this laptop.
questions.correct_explanation: In hosted (Type 2) virtualization, the hypervisor runs as software on top of an ordinary host operating system, as on this laptop, and each virtual machine runs its own guest system. Bare metal (Type 1) is the runner-up: it is what cloud data centers use, but there the hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host operating system underneath.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: bare metal hypervisors run most cloud servers. But they sit directly on the hardware, with no ordinary operating system underneath, unlike this laptop.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because containers also isolate workloads. But containers share the host's kernel and run no guest operating system, while this test machine runs its own.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is another way to run workloads. But serverless code runs on a provider's managed platform, not inside an app on a laptop.

tips: Eliminate: B shares the host's kernel and runs no guest system, and C is code run on a provider's platform, not a laptop app.
Final two: D beats A because this hypervisor runs on top of the laptop's operating system, while bare metal runs directly on the hardware.
Exam cue: a hypervisor on the hardware is bare metal (Type 1); a hypervisor on a host operating system is hosted (Type 2).
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-125 Section 2.2 (Types of Full Virtualization: a bare metal hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, while a hosted hypervisor runs on top of the host OS)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, as in cloud data centers; a Type 2 hypervisor runs on an ordinary operating system' (notes 4.3.2 Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A symphony is moving its donor database from a server it ran itself to a managed database service, a platform as a service (PaaS). Which task MOST clearly stays with the symphony's IT team?

options.A: Setting who may query the database and from which networks
options.B: Patching the database software and the system it runs on
options.C: Replacing failed disks in the provider's storage hardware
options.D: Nothing further, since the provider now runs the database

questions.key_concept: In PaaS the provider maintains the platform software; the customer still controls its data, access rights and service settings.
questions.pre_read: Split the database into the platform that runs it and the data inside it.
questions.correct_explanation: In PaaS, the provider runs and patches the platform, including the database software and the operating system beneath it, while the customer keeps its data, access rights and service settings, such as who may connect and from where. Patching the database software is the runner-up: it was the team's job on its own server, but on PaaS the provider takes it on.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the team did patch the database on its own server. But in PaaS the provider maintains the database software and the system under it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the data lives on those disks. But physical hardware is always the provider's job in a cloud service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider now runs the platform. But the customer still owns its data, accounts, access rights and settings in every service model.

tips: Eliminate: C is physical hardware, always the provider's, and D forgets that access and settings stay with the customer in every model.
Final two: A beats B because PaaS providers maintain the database software, while who may reach the data stays a customer setting.
Exam cue: in PaaS, the provider runs the platform; the customer secures its code, data, access and settings.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'PaaS offers a managed runtime, database or development platform; the customer secures its own code and settings' (notes 4.3.3 Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bagel chain spreads its services across three public cloud providers so it does not depend on any one of them. Which security task does this MOST clearly add for the IT coordinator?

options.A: Securing the link that moves data between its private and public clouds
options.B: Sharing infrastructure with other firms that follow the same rules
options.C: Buying and running its own data center hardware for the services
options.D: Keeping settings the same in several separate admin consoles

questions.key_concept: Multi-cloud reduces reliance on one provider but adds more consoles and settings to keep consistently secure; hybrid joins different deployment models.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changes when the same work spreads across several providers.
questions.correct_explanation: Using several public providers is multi-cloud: it cuts reliance on any one provider, but each has its own console, settings and defaults, so keeping security settings consistent across them is the added work. Securing a private-to-public link is the runner-up: that is a hybrid cloud's task, where distinct clouds are bound together, and this chain runs no private cloud.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: links between joined clouds do need securing in a hybrid cloud. But this chain uses only public providers, with no private cloud to link.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because several parties are involved. But sharing infrastructure with organizations under common rules describes a community cloud, not one firm using three providers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because spreading out sounds like more infrastructure. But public cloud customers run no data center hardware; that burden comes with a private cloud on their own site.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a community cloud, and C describes running a private cloud on site, while this chain uses public providers.
Final two: D beats A because several public providers multiply the settings to secure, while a private-to-public link belongs to a hybrid cloud.
Exam cue: multi-cloud means several providers and more settings to keep consistent; hybrid means joined deployment models and links to secure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: deployment models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Hybrid cloud and multi-cloud mean the same thing' (exam trap, notes 4.3.4 Cloud Deployment Models). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A talent agency's client files leaked after its cloud provider's own staff misconfigured the storage service, and the owner asks who must answer to the clients. Which reply from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: The provider, because the files were stored on its platform
options.B: The provider, because its own staff made the mistake
options.C: The agency and provider equally, since accountability is shared
options.D: The agency, because accountability for its data stays with it

questions.key_concept: Moving data to the cloud shares duties but not accountability; the customer stays accountable for its data even when the provider errs.
questions.pre_read: Separate who caused the leak from who answers to the clients.
questions.correct_explanation: Contracts can share security duties, but an organization stays accountable for the security and privacy of its data in the cloud, so the agency answers to its clients; it can then seek remedies from the provider under the contract. The provider's mistake is the runner-up: it makes the provider answerable to the agency, not a replacement for the agency's own accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the files sat on the provider's platform. But where data is stored does not move accountability for it away from the organization.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the provider did cause the leak and may owe the agency remedies. But the agency still answers to its own clients for data it chose to put there.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because security duties are shared. But duties can be divided while accountability for the data stays with the organization.

tips: Eliminate: A ties accountability to where data is stored, and C confuses shared duties with shared accountability.
Final two: D beats B because a provider's fault makes it answerable to the agency, while the agency stays accountable to its clients.
Exam cue: duties can be outsourced; accountability for the data stays with the organization that owns it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-144 Section 2.3 (Outsourcing and Accountability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Moving to the cloud transfers accountability for a data breach to the provider' (exam trap, notes 4.3.5 The Shared Responsibility Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud roles and agreements
questions.question: An estate agency's IT coordinator buys storage, email and backup from one firm that combines three providers' services and negotiates with them on the agency's behalf. Which NIST cloud actor is the firm MOST accurately?

options.A: A cloud provider
options.B: A cloud auditor
options.C: A cloud carrier
options.D: A cloud broker

questions.key_concept: NIST's cloud broker manages and combines cloud services and negotiates between providers and consumers; carriers supply connectivity.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose services the firm is actually selling.
questions.correct_explanation: In NIST's cloud reference architecture, a cloud broker manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates relationships between providers and consumers, often combining several providers' services into one. The provider is the runner-up: a provider makes its own service available, while this firm assembles and manages other providers' services.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the agency does buy its services from this firm. But the firm combines other providers' services and negotiates with them, which NIST calls brokering.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the firm keeps an eye on the services it manages. But a cloud auditor conducts independent assessments of cloud services; it does not sell or manage them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the services reach the agency through the firm. But a cloud carrier provides connectivity and transport, such as network links, not service packages.

tips: Eliminate: B assesses cloud services independently, and C provides the network connectivity that carries cloud services.
Final two: D beats A because the firm combines and manages other providers' services and negotiates with them, rather than offering its own.
Exam cue: combining and negotiating for others is a broker; carrying traffic is a carrier; checking independently is an auditor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 500-292 Section 2.5 (Cloud Broker: manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates relationships between providers and consumers)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'NIST names the five actors; one organization can play several' (notes 4.3.6 Cloud Roles and Agreements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ramen chain's data owner labels its AI training data Restricted; procedure has the system administrator encrypt Restricted buckets with the customer-managed key. What should the administrator do FIRST about that data's unencrypted bucket?

options.A: Report the unencrypted bucket to the data owner and await a decision
options.B: Encrypt the bucket with the customer-managed key, and record it
options.C: Delete the bucket's files, as unencrypted data is already exposed
options.D: Encrypt the bucket with the provider-managed key, and record it

questions.key_concept: Protecting the customer's data, AI training data included, is the customer's job in every cloud model, so apply the encryption the procedure assigns.
questions.pre_read: Check what the data owner and the procedure have already decided.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner has already classified the data, and the procedure gives this exact fix to the administrator, so they encrypt the bucket with the customer-managed key and record the change. Reporting to the data owner is the runner-up: they own the data and its classification, but their decision is already made, and the procedure under it assigns the encryption step.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the data owner does own the training data. But they have already classified it, and the procedure assigns this encryption step to the administrator.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because exposed data feels urgent. But unencrypted is not the same as public, deleting destroys data the business needs, and copies may remain in backups.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a provider-managed key also encrypts the bucket. But the procedure names the customer-managed key, which keeps key control with the chain rather than the provider.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes training data the business needs instead of protecting it, and D uses the provider-managed key, which leaves key control with the provider when the procedure names the customer's key.
Final two: B beats A because the owner's classification and the procedure already decide this step, so the administrator carries it out.
Exam cue: in every cloud model, protecting and keying the customer's own data is the customer's job, so look for the customer-side step the procedure already names.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.7 (Data Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Classify, encrypt, control the keys and back up: the data is the customer's job in every model' (notes 4.3.7 Protecting Data in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud access security brokers
questions.question: A paint store chain's IT manager says its new cloud access security broker (CASB) just repeats what the network firewall already does. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: A CASB sees which cloud apps staff use and applies data rules
options.B: A CASB filters cloud traffic by IP address and port number
options.C: A CASB blocks web pages by category, such as gambling sites
options.D: A CASB encrypts the traffic between the stores and head office

questions.key_concept: A CASB sits between users and cloud services to reveal app use, shadow IT included, and enforce data rules; web filters only sort sites.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each tool can see that the others cannot.
questions.correct_explanation: A CASB sits between users and cloud services, so it can show which cloud apps staff use, including unapproved ones, and enforce data rules on them, which a firewall filtering by network rules cannot. Category-based web filtering is the runner-up: it also sits in the path, but it sorts sites, not what users do inside cloud apps.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both sit in the traffic path. But filtering by address and port is a firewall rule, even for cloud traffic; a CASB understands cloud apps, users and data.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: many CASBs do sit in the path like a web proxy. But sorting sites by category shows nothing of what staff do or move inside cloud apps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both protect traffic. But encrypting links between sites is a VPN's job, not a broker's view into cloud app use.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a network firewall's rules, and D describes a site-to-site VPN; neither understands cloud apps and data.
Final two: A beats C because a CASB understands cloud apps, users and data, while a web filter only sorts sites by category.
Exam cue: a CASB sees inside cloud app use (who, which app, which data); firewalls and web filters see addresses, ports and sites.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-215 Section 3.1 (Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A CASB does the same job as a network firewall' (exam trap, notes 4.3.8 Cloud Misconfiguration, CSPM and CASB). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sports analytics startup wants to deploy a third-party model from its cloud AI platform's public catalog, which the provider offers as is, without review. Who MOST clearly must vet the model before use?

options.A: The startup, since it chooses which models it deploys
options.B: The provider, since the model sits in its catalog
options.C: The model's uploader, since the startup did not build it
options.D: No one, since popular open models are checked by their users

questions.key_concept: On a cloud AI platform, the provider secures the platform, and the customer must vet the third-party models it chooses to deploy.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decides which model goes into use.
questions.correct_explanation: Shared responsibility for AI follows the service model: the provider secures the platform, while the customer owns the data, models and settings it chooses to use, so a third-party model offered as is must be vetted by the startup, like any outside component. The provider is the runner-up: it hosts the catalog, but it has said plainly that it does not review these models.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the provider does secure the platform and its catalog service. But it offers these third-party models as is, so checking them falls to the customer that deploys them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because authors know their own models. But an unknown uploader owes the startup nothing, and the startup carries the risk of whatever it deploys.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because popular models feel proven. But downloads are not a security review, and tampered or poisoned models can look like ordinary ones.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on an unknown uploader who owes the startup nothing, and D treats popularity as if it were a security review.
Final two: A beats B because the provider offers catalog models as is; the customer owns the models it chooses to run.
Exam cue: on a cloud AI platform, the provider secures the platform, and the customer secures the models and data it brings or picks.
